problem.text: How many sequences of $0$s and $1$s of length $19$ are there that begin with a $0$, end with a $0$, contain no two consecutive $0$s, and contain no three consecutive $1$s?

steps.title: Where to start: what can come after a $0$?
steps.body: Both rules are about runs: $0$s can never touch, and $1$s come in runs of length at most $2$. So after any $0$ that is not the last digit, the next $0$ comes after a run of one or two $1$s. That means a valid sequence is a single $0$ followed by blocks, each block being $10$ or $110$.

your_turn.prompt: Why can a block not be just $0$ or $1110$?
your_turn.answer: A block $0$ would put two $0$s next to each other, and $1110$ contains three consecutive $1$s.

steps.title: Set up the recursion
steps.body:
Let $a_n$ be the number of valid sequences of length $n$ (starting and ending with $0$). Look at the last block: removing a final $10$ leaves a valid sequence of length $n-2$, and removing a final $110$ leaves one of length $n-3$. Adding either block to a valid sequence always gives a valid one, so
$$a_n = a_{n-2} + a_{n-3}$$

your_turn.answer: Each is $1$: $010$, $0110$, and $01010$ (the other candidate $01110$ has three $1$s in a row).

steps.title: Build up the table
steps.body: Now $a_6 = a_4 + a_3 = 2$, $a_7 = a_5 + a_4 = 2$, $a_8 = a_6 + a_5 = 3$, $a_9 = 4$ and $a_{10} = 5$. Careful: the rule skips back two and three places, so $a_n$ does not use $a_{n-1}$ at all.
